parts.visual:
We are taught to seek 'Win-Win' negotiations. But in high-stakes corporate deals, many negotiations are 'Zero-Sum': For me to gain a dollar, you must lose a dollar.

The Dark Arts of Zero-Sum:
1. The Anchor: Making the first offer aggressively high/low to psychologically control the rest of the math.
2. The Flinch: Feigning shock and outrage at the other party's offer to make them feel unreasonable.
3. The Walk-Away: He who cares less about the outcome holds all the power.
parts.audio: In high-stakes corporate deals, negotiations are often Zero-Sum. For you to win, the other party must lose. Master the Anchor and the Walk-Away to dominate.

questions.question: You are selling your company. You want $50 Million. The buyer asks for your price. What is the 'Anchoring' strategy?
options: Say 'We will not accept anything less than 80 Million.' This aggressively shifts the psychological baseline so that when you eventually 'compromise' at 60 Million, you still win.
Ask them what they want to pay.
questions.correct_answer: Say 'We will not accept anything less than 80 Million.' This aggressively shifts the psychological baseline so that when you eventually 'compromise' at 60 Million, you still win.
questions.explanation: The first number spoken in a negotiation permanently anchors all future math. He who speaks first, sets the anchor.

questions.question: Listen to the negotiator. What psychological tactic is this?
questions.tts_text: Are you out of your mind? That offer is actively insulting to the intelligence of my board. We are done here.
questions.explanation: If you act desperate for the deal, you lose. By acting outraged and threatening to leave, you force the other side to panic and offer more.

questions.question: What is BATNA?
options: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement. It is your 'Plan B'. If your Plan B is strong, you have massive power.
questions.correct_answer: Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement. It is your 'Plan B'. If your Plan B is strong, you have massive power.
questions.explanation: If you don't need the deal to survive (strong BATNA), you can negotiate ruthlessly. If you will go bankrupt without the deal (weak BATNA), you will be crushed.

questions.question: In a Zero-Sum negotiation, why should you never 'split the difference' (meet in the middle)?
options: Because the other party likely set an aggressive 'Anchor'. If you meet in the middle of a fake number, you still lose.
questions.correct_answer: Because the other party likely set an aggressive 'Anchor'. If you meet in the middle of a fake number, you still lose.
questions.explanation: Splitting the difference is for amateurs. Professionals negotiate based on leverage and data.

questions.explanation: The ultimate display of leverage. You cannot bluff this; you must mean it.
